Hankook tipped to enter race for F1 tyre supply contract
article_text:
It's another vivid demonstration of Formula 1's ever-growing global reach and popularity that another serious contender has emerged to bid for its exclusive tyre-supply contract.

Pirelli took over from Bridgestone as F1's sole tyre supplier in 2011 and for much of its first decade it faced little in the way of concerted challenge when renewal time rolled around. That has changed in recent years. Having walked away from F1 in 2010, citing costs and a "strategic realignment" following the global financial crisis, Bridgestone threw its hat in the ring during the most recent tender process in 2023, and is known to be preparing a pitch for the next one.

Now Motorsport.com understands that Hankook, exclusive tyre supplier to the World Rally Championship, is assembling a bid for the tender process which opens next year for the post-2028 F1 era. It was previously an unsuccessful bidder in 2018 for the contract covering 2020-23, which was then extended by a year owing to the pandemic.

Pirelli's current contract runs from 2025-28, since the company – along with the FIA and F1 – mutually exercised a one-year extension clause last June. During the last tender process, technical stability during the transition to a new formula this season was regarded as a particularly important. Given the impending changes in 2030, potential bidders will have to assure the FIA they can achieve this.

While the FIA assesses tenders based on the bidder's technical capacity, sustainability credentials, and the operational capacity to manage the supply process seamlessly, F1 also has a voice in the final decision on commercial grounds. Pirelli is a conspicuously big spender on trackside signage as well as facilitating VIP perks such as the ‘Hot Laps' programme.

Hankook has already played a small role in grand prix weekends as a supplier to the W Series in 2021 and 2022. The South Korean company has been involved in motor racing for over three decades, at various times being exclusive supplier to the DTM, along with regional F3 and F4 series. It supplied Formula E's Gen3-era cars from 2022-26 before Bridgestone took on that contract.

It was appointed sole tyre supplier of the World Rally Championship in 2025 and this year it was named by the FIA as a member of the governing body's ‘global partner programme'.

Representatives including Hankook Competition CEO Steven Cho have attended several grands prix over the past two seasons, most recently last weekend in Las Vegas. It's understood the company has already conducted testing of prototype tyres with an F2-based ‘mule car', and that more testing is planned with a specific focus on wet-weather tyres with a narrower spray plume.

Racing in the wet is currently problematic because, while the 'extreme' wets are highly efficient at displacing surface water, the spray that ensues tends to reduce visibility to the point where a red flag is inevitable.

Having supplied two major FIA world championships in recent years, along with establishing much closer ties with the governing body, it would make this a much more credible bid than the previous one. Formula E is a strong calling card since its environmental aims call for just two different tyre compounds, both made from sustainable materials. Sustainability was Pirelli's finishing move in the last tender process, since it undertook to introduce Forest Stewardship Council-certified tyres to F1 from 2024 onwards.

Although based in South Korea, Hankook has an R&D facility in Hanover, Germany, and a factory in Hungary currently undergoing a €450million expansion in Hungary. Pirelli makes its motorsport products, including the F1 tyres, alongside regular road tyres in its factory in Izmit, Turkey.

A 44-person internal taskforce has already been assembled for the project, Motorsport.com understands.

Any company entering the tender process faces a significant challenge because it will be bidding to arrive in year four of the current technical regulations, so it would have to build a very convincing case that it could at least match the existing product. While Pirelli's tyres have come in for regular criticism over the years, this is in the nature of having exclusivity.

The current tyres are expected to deliver on a complex and often contradictory set of requirements: they must be thermally and structurally robust, but with a predictable degradation curve to facilitate the spectacle and strategic variety. Experience of the past 15 years demonstrates how easy it is to overshoot either way.

"Pirelli has been an important partner to the FIA F1 world championship for many years, providing a consistently high standard of performance, innovation and safety at the highest level of our sport," said FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem when the contact extension was announced in June. "This extension through to the end of 2028 provides stability for the championship."

That, along with the prevalence of Pirelli branding around the tracks, paints a clear picture of what any bidder has to offer: deep pockets, and a guarantee that when their tyres go on, nobody will notice any difference apart from the name on the sidewalls.

Sesame becomes the new Main Sponsor of Levante UD
article_text:
The leading comprehensive platform in talent and human resources management supports the club for the entire season.

Levante UD and Sesame, the leading comprehensive platform for talent and human resources management, have reached a sponsorship agreement through which the Valencian technology company becomes the Main Sponsor of the club starting from the 2026/27 season.

As the main sponsor of the men's first team, Sesame will feature on the front of the official game jersey as we already saw a few days ago with the launch of the first and second kits, on training gear, and on other physical and digital assets of the club. The agreement also includes a comprehensive program of activations, VIP experiences, corporate events, and content initiatives that will bring the brand closer to fans and the business community.

For Sesame, this sponsorship represents a key step in its brand positioning and visibility, associating itself with one of the historic clubs of Spanish football and a benchmark in Valencian sports. Additionally, this agreement reflects a growing trend in which high-growth technology companies seek to connect their brands with spaces capable of generating community, belonging, and shared emotions. For the company, football represents an environment where values such as teamwork, perseverance, and talent development are experienced every day.

“This alliance with Levante UD makes perfect sense for us. Football and scale-ups like Sesame have much more in common than it seems. Both of us thrive on building teams, developing talent, making quick decisions, and competing every day to improve. At Sesame, we believe that this way of understanding growth deserves to go beyond offices and connect with millions of people,” stated Albert Soriano, CEO of Sesame.

The head of Sesame also emphasized the local nature of the collaboration. “We are especially excited that this agreement is with a club from our homeland. We are a tech company born in Valencia that now works with companies all over the world, and we are very proud of our origins as well as being able to support Levante UD,” added Soriano.

For Levante UD, it is a great satisfaction to be associated with and display on their chest the brand of a Valencian technology company that is a leader in the field of human resources. “The arrival of Sesame as the main sponsor reinforces our commitment to innovation, professionalism, and continuing to grow hand in hand with companies that are transforming their sectors from Valencia to the world,” stated Pablo Sánchez, president of Levante UD.

Following the announcement of this agreement, Sesame and Levante UD are opening a new phase of collaboration in which various joint actions are planned, as well as the promotion of projects that go beyond sports sponsorship, bringing innovation, technology, sports, and the values of talent closer to Levante fans and society as a whole.

Sesame is human resources software focused on redefining the employee experience. It allows the digitalization of the most routine human resources processes so that managers and HR professionals can focus on talent, professional development, and the well-being of their teams, thereby growing their business and building a successful corporate culture. Currently, they have more than 20,000 clients in over 30 countries across Europe and Latin America.

title: Six sports federations sound the alarm about the future of Bulgarian sport over the amendments to the Gambling Act
article_text:
Six of Bulgaria's leading sports federations have issued a joint position against some of the proposed amendments to the Gambling Act. Among them is the Bulgarian Volleyball Federation, which, together with the organizations governing football, basketball, athletics, aquatic sports and tennis, is urging members of parliament to reconsider the restrictions affecting sports sponsorship.

The reaction was prompted by the advanced stage of the legislative process. On 18 November, the National Assembly adopted at first reading three bills amending and supplementing the Gambling Act, and on 19 November they were merged into a single bill, number 52-653-01-51. The lead committee on it is the parliamentary Committee on Budget and Finance.

The federations support measures against gambling addiction, including the ban on placing gambling operators' brands on children's sports kit and the restriction of outdoor advertising outside sports facilities.

Their main objection is to limiting sponsors' ability to promote their partnerships with sports organizations. According to the federations, this would render a large share of existing contracts economically meaningless and would lead to them being reduced or terminated.

Particularly vulnerable under such a scenario would be clubs in small towns and villages, where opportunities to attract alternative advertisers are limited. The consequences could affect not only professional sport, but also youth academies, coaches' salaries and the maintenance of sports infrastructure.

The timing of the six federations' joint position is key to the legislative process. It is precisely today, 27 November, that the official deadline for submitting proposed amendments to the merged bill before its second reading expires.

On 19 November, at the proposal of MP Konstantin Prodanov, parliament extended the deadline from seven to eight days. The decision was supported by 128 MPs, with 11 voting against and three abstaining.

After the deadline expires, the Committee on Budget and Finance must review the proposals received and prepare a report for the second vote in the plenary chamber.

As of the evening of 27 November, no date has yet been set in the National Assembly's official agenda for the second reading of the bill. Nor has a meeting of the lead Committee on Budget and Finance been announced to consider the proposals received. The next regular plenary sittings are expected on 2, 3 and 4 December, but their agenda has not yet been published.

How did the amendments to the Gambling Act come about?

- 4 September 2026 – a bill submitted by Venko Sabrutev and a group of MPs.

- 9 September 2026 – a bill submitted by Bozhidar Bozhanov and a group of MPs.

- 23 September 2026 – the Ministry of Finance opens a public consultation on its draft.

- 23 October 2026 – the public consultation ends.

- 5 November 2026 – a summary of the submitted opinions is published.

- 11 November 2026 – the Council of Ministers submits its bill to Parliament.

- 12 November 2026 – the budget committee unanimously supports all three bills with 21 votes "in favour" each.

- 18 November 2026 – Parliament adopts the bills at first reading.

- 19 November 2026 – a consolidated bill is drafted.

- 27 November 2026 – the deadline for proposals ahead of the second reading expires.

The public consultation on the government bill lasted one month. It has not been established whether the six sports federations now coming out with a joint position took part in it with their own submissions.

A particularly important detail left out of the federations' joint declaration is the mechanism for additional funding of Bulgarian sport provided for in the government bill.

The proposal is for the variable part of the state fee on online betting to be increased from 20% to 21% in 2027 and to 22% from the beginning of 2028.

The additional one and two percentage points may be ceded to gambling operators on condition that the funds are channelled through sponsorship or donations to licensed sports federations, registered sports clubs, the Bulgarian Olympic Committee and the National Paralympic Organisation. However, the funding is limited to non-commercial activities in sport.

An increase in contributions for socially responsible conduct is also envisaged, with the expected revenue of 15.7 million euros to be distributed equally among the ministries of sport, health and education.

The key question is whether these mechanisms will be able to offset a possible outflow of funds from current sponsorship agreements. The federations' joint position does not specify a concrete amount of the expected financial losses.

Reports from the parliamentary committee make it clear that the Ministry of Youth and Sports supports the fight against gambling addiction, but at the same time warns of a possible decline in revenue.

The Bulgarian Sports Totalizator has also proposed amendments to the legislative texts, while the Council for Electronic Media has raised the need to assess the effect of the restrictions introduced back in 2024.

When considering the bills, MPs agreed to set up a working group with representatives of institutions, business and experts to seek balanced solutions.

The combined bill still contains three alternative versions of Article 10 of the Gambling Act, which regulates advertising.

The government's version allows sponsors to be displayed on the official websites of the sponsored organisations, but prohibits additional digital display of their brands during television and online broadcasts of sporting events.

The second option is considerably more restrictive. It provides that the logo of a gambling operator on sports kit be limited to 10 by 10 centimetres, and the kit must be intended for adults.

Why F1 Races Get Shorter in 2027, and How the 305km Rule Came to Be
article_text:
Formula 1 races will become shorter in 2027, with the standard distance falling from 305km to 290km. That means most Grands Prix will lose two or three laps, depending on the circuit.

The change is tied to planned fuel-flow adjustments in the 2027 power-unit rules. F1 will allow more fuel to flow through the engines, which means cars need more fuel to finish a race. Teams designed their 2026 fuel tanks around the current rules and want to avoid building new chassis.

- Formula 1 will temporarily reduce grand prix distances to 290 kilometers in 2027 due to changes in power unit regulations. This adjustment is a short-term measure, as the FIA plans to revert to the standard 305 kilometers in 2028.… pic.twitter.com/XPj9lJC01c

That created a problem for teams planning to carry over their existing cars. Officials first considered cutting selected races, but different distances risked turning some events into fuel-saving runs. Instead, they agreed to reduce almost every Grand Prix to the same 290km target.

The engine changes will also shift the balance between electric and combustion power. In 2027, combustion power will provide 58% of the total, while electric power will provide 42%. Fuel flow will increase by 5%, before another increase in 2028 moves the split to 60-40.

The change will only last for one season. The FIA's published regulations already set the standard distance back at 305km for 2028. Monaco will keep its separate 260km distance.

F1 did not always follow one fixed race distance. From 1950 to 1957, races had to cover more than 300km or run for three hours. The rules changed again in 1966, when race distances were set between 300km and 400km.

In 1971, the maximum distance was cut to 321.87km, or 200 miles. The 305km standard arrived in 1989, setting the race length fans came to know. Since then, Grands Prix have used the fewest complete laps needed to exceed 305km.

The distance rule has also had to work across very different circuits. A lap at a short track covers far less ground than a lap at a long one, so each Grand Prix needs a different lap count. The distance target gives the championship one shared standard, even when the number of laps changes from race to race.

The 2027 change shows how closely race distances remain tied to technical rules. Fuel flow, tank size, and car design have always helped decide how much racing fans get to watch.

The 2027 season will bring more changes beyond the shorter race distance. The FIA has also agreed to changes affecting race delays, practice sessions, and gearbox development.

Races disrupted by rain or other delays will follow a new hard stop time. The current three-hour limit, which includes interruptions, will be removed. However, the limit of two hours of actual racing will remain.

Race control will also have more freedom to extend practice sessions after interruptions. This should give teams more time on track when delays affect their running. Gearbox homologation will also be removed for 2027. This will give gearbox suppliers more freedom to develop their designs.

A new chapter for FIA Formula 1 officiating.

From 2027, the FIA will begin introducing full-time stewards to the FIA Formula One World Championship, strengthening consistency, expertise and continuity in race decision-making.

Building towards a department of 12–15 full-time… pic.twitter.com/xHQZ92rAz8

The FIA will also begin bringing in full-time stewards during the 2027 season. They will work alongside existing officials, with the aim of improving consistency in race decisions.

The Sprint calendar will additionally grow from six events to ten. Portugal and Turkey will also return, while the championship will keep its 24-race schedule across 22 countries.

title: Bodø/Glimt lead global football clubs with 555 per cent social media growth in 2026
article_text:
Bodø/Glimt recorded the highest percentage increase in social media followers among the world’s leading football clubs in 2026, with their combined Instagram and TikTok audience increasing by 555 per cent between 1st January and 17th November, according to data platform Football Benchmark.

The club’s following grew from approximately 136,000 to 888,000, placing them at the top of Football Benchmark’s ranking of the ten fastest-growing clubs by percentage. Their 555 per cent growth rate was more than 2.7 times that of Chicago Fire FC, the second-ranked club, which recorded an increase of 205 per cent, with Turkish side Trabzonspor registering 140 per cent growth closing in the first three clubs with the biggest digital increase. Also worth highlighting is the contrast with Como 1907, the emerging force in Italian football, which ranked fourth with 138 per cent growth – more than five times lower than Bodø/Glimt’s figure. The analysis took into account only clubs with at least 100k total followers across Instagram and TikTok.

Having competed in Norway’s second division as recently as 2017, Bodø/Glimt have transformed their sporting standing through sustained development and consistent performances on the European stage. Last season’s Uefa Champions League campaign, featuring victories over Manchester City and Atlético de Madrid before eliminating Inter, further elevated the club’s international profile.

The figures demonstrate how sporting performance and European competition exposure can accelerate international audience growth, creating opportunities to strengthen brand positioning, expand commercial reach and attract new partners.

Bodø/Glimt’s achievement also highlights the changing dynamics of football’s global attention economy, where ambitious clubs can build significant international audiences through sporting credibility and a distinctive competitive identity, challenging the traditional dominance of established football brands.

Source: Football Benchmark Social Media Analytics Platform. Combined Instagram and TikTok followers, 1 January–17 November 2026.

Empower Sports is a global PR Agency that builds and boosts the brand of clubs, executives, coaches and athletes.

title: F1 Qatar GP: Antonelli leads Russell in opening practice
article_text:
Newly crowned world champion Kimi Antonelli has comfortably topped first practice at Formula 1's Qatar Grand Prix, holding off Mercedes team-mate George Russell as drivers grappled with the tricky Lusail circuit.

One week on from the high-speed drag race on the streets of Las Vegas, drivers and teams were facing a completely different challenge as they sampled the high downforce motorcycle track of Lusail.

In the opening stages of the first hour of practice on the smooth swoops of the Doha track, they deployed both Pirelli's medium and hard tyre compounds to get the lay of the land and gather data.

This year's world champion Antonelli led all the way through, setting an early benchmark of 1m24.057s on mediums and then gradually chipping away on subsequent run, establishing a 1m23.217s lap after 20-odd minutes to head Mercedes team-mate Russell by seven tenths.

The Mercedes pair led the cars of Red Bull, McLaren and Ferrari as they populated the leaderboard two by two, until teams started switching to the soft-tyre compound at the halfway point.

But despite deploying the softer and faster tyre compounds, Antonelli's early benchmark proved tough to topple. Russell, who was experimenting with different wing configurations, came short by half a second, while Antonelli also couldn't touch his own medium-tyre lap as the Lusail surface became littered with gravel from the many off-track excursions.

In the Red Bull Isack Hadjar set third, 0.661 in arrears, followed by a nervous looking pair of McLaren cars in the hands of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri, who both conceded eight tenths, and Las Vegas winner Max Verstappen.

Ferrari was the fourth-fastest team after a muted session, with Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton over 1.2s adrift from Antonelli after grappling with massive front tyre degradation.

Racing Bulls rookie Arvid Lindblad led the midfield aboard the VCARB 03, with Alpine's Pierre Gasly rounding out the top 10.

title: Campus Activewear signs Rugged Rush deal, plans obstacle racing shoe
The Inside Story on the Mercedes-AMG Petronas F1 Team’s Triumphant Season
article_text:
Last week, motorsport’s controlled maelstrom that is Formula 1 descended on Las Vegas for the 21st grand prix of the 2026 season. Yet the biggest questions, namely, who would secure the Constructors’ crown and the Drivers’ Championship title had already been answered by the Mercedes-AMG Petronas F1 team and its young phenom Kimi Antonelli, respectively.

Prior to Friday’s qualifying session, Bradley Lord, deputy team principal for the Mercedes squad, visited our House of Robb Las Vegas Grand Prix pop-up, located at the Allē Lounge on the 66th Floor of Resorts World. There, the second-in-command under Toto Wolff discussed why success came so decisively this season and shared insights on the team’s drivers, the tactical approach for the remainder of the season, and how the world’s premier race series has become a thriving business.

“It’s completely transformed in the last decade, from a niche sport of enthusiasts racing around the world to, you know, one of the biggest and fastest growing sports in the world, with a vastly different footprint, vastly different profile, and with that, the revenue that we’re able to generate as a team has expanded enormously,” Lord told the audience. “This year, we should hit $1 billion in revenue for the very first time, which is quite amazing for a small manufacturing company in the middle of the U.K.,” he mentioned regarding the team’s financial renaissance.

More impressive than the recent fiscal performance of Mercedes, though, has been its dominance in Formula 1 since 2014, when it began a winning streak of Constructors’ Championship titles that continued through 2021. Not only was that a legacy-defining span for the team, but also for its star driver Lewis Hamilton, who finished first in the Drivers’ Championship six of those seasons, bringing his total—so far—to seven.

The past four years have been decidedly more challenging for the Silver Arrows, especially with the series swapping to ground-effect cars, leaving Red Bull Racing and McLaren taking turns at the top. In 2025, Mercedes won only two races, while George Russell and Kimi Antonelli ended the season in fourth and seventh, respectively. This season, Antonelli had earned enough points by the end of the Mexico City Grand Prix to be crowned the overall victor, and Mercedes—winning 12 races—was the undisputed Constructors’ Champion after the contest in Brazil on November 8. So, what changed?

“Periodically in Formula 1, every sort of four five years, we have a major rules change . . . usually designed to slow the cars down, because every year they get faster, and at some point they get unsafe for the circuits we race on,” explained Lord. “And for 2026, we changed both the power units, so changed the engines—still 1.6-liter V-6 turbos, but with much more electrical energy as part of the overall power, so we’ve got over 1000 hp. Roughly 50 percent of that comes from an electric motor, 50 percent of it from the combustion engine; and around that new power unit, we put new aerodynamic regulations.” According to Lord, adapting to the new protocols also necessitated that the chassis, electronic control unit, and tires were all new as well.

The herculean course change for the cars also required reimagining what would feed the internal-combustion engines in order to complement the environmental ethos of hybridization. “Developing an advanced sustainable fuel means also developing all the infrastructure to produce that fuel as well. So that’s been an enormous job,” said Lord. “So we did the opposite of what you were always taught in chemistry or in physics at school, which is, if you do an experiment, change one thing at a time. We ripped up everything at the same time and landed with a new formula for 2026.” Of the shift in parameters dictated by Formula 1, Lord summed up the obvious by noting; “We have done a better job than the other teams in navigating that rule set.”

The transformation of Kimi Antonelli, who landed on the team’s radar when he was only around 11 years old (such was his karting prowess), has been more compelling to witness. Selected to fill the seat Hamilton vacated to join Ferrari, Antonelli had a rookie year that more than hinted at his potential, but few could have anticipated what would follow.

“It seems crazy to think that Kimi only won his first race, and got his first pole position, in China this year at the second race of the season,” said Lord. “From there, he went on a run of wins . . . five in a row that set himself up for an unexpected but quite remarkable championship challenge—he’s done all that at the age of 20, and so he’s become the first Italian champion in 73 years.” Equally noteworthy for Lord is how the young driver has handled it all. “He’s managed to both deliver something very, very exceptional, but also keep his feet on the ground and stay incredibly humble, grounded, and in touch with reality at the same time.”

His teammate George Russell’s experience, despite winning the Australian Grand Prix in March to start it all off, has been markedly different. “George has had both the strongest and the most disappointing season of his career,” mentioned Lord. “He’s had the lion’s share of the technical problems we’ve had. We’ve had a lot of unreliability in this first season with the new cars and the new engines, and he has struggled with that more than Kimi . . . he’s had a season that’s really tested his resilience.”
